tone_statements.citation: Hagège, Claude. 1967. Description phonologique du parler wori (sud-ouest du Cameroun). Journal of West African Languages 4(2): 15-34.
tone_statements.quote: L'impossibilité de trouver sur un monosyllabe une opposition entre trois tons ponctuels dont aucun ne soit le résultat d'une neutralisation nous a fait considérer que le wori est une langue à tons normalement ponctuels, au nombre de deux. Ces deux registres fondamentaux, haut et bas, donnent quatre possibilités distinctives, comme le montrent les exemples qui précèdent. Nous avons appelé “tons mélodiques simples” les deux combinaisons registre haut-registre bas et registre bas-registre haut, ce qui ne doit pas faire conclure à l'existence de 4 tons en wori, mais signifie seulement que la succession des deux tons ponctuels de cette langue dans le cadre d'une même syllabe a valeur distinctive.
tone_statements.translation: The impossibility of finding, on a monosyllable, an opposition between three level tones none of which is the result of a neutralisation has led us to consider Wori a language with normally level tones, two in number. These two basic registers, high and low, yield four distinctive possibilities, as the preceding examples show. We have called 'simple melodic tones' the two combinations high register-low register and low register-high register, which must not lead one to conclude that there are 4 tones in Wori, but means only that the succession of the two level tones of this language within a single syllable has distinctive value.

sources.note: Lists Duala dialects after Maho (2009): Duala proper, Bodiman, Oli (Ewodi, Wuri), Pongo, Mongo; says Duala is a tonal language; nothing on stress. Phonology refs cited: Paulian 1971 (Esquisse phonologique du duala, Études bantoues I, SELAF, 53-88) and Helmlinger 1972 — both Duala proper.

sources.citation: Ebobissé, Carl. 1989. Dialectométrie lexicale des parlers sawabantu. Journal of West African Languages 19(2): 57-66.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone. Lexicostatistic (dialectometric) comparison of 15 coastal varieties incl. 'l'oli' and 'le bidiman' (A.25 Oli in Guthrie; bidiman absent from Guthrie); result p. 62: subgroup '5. oli-bidiman' among seven subgroups; oli shares 58.3% with duala although geographically closest to it up the Wouri (p. 62). First-hand data on the variety, but no phonology.

sources.citation: Dinkelacker, Ernst. 1914. Wörterbuch der Duala-Sprache. Abhandlungen des Hamburgischen Kolonialinstituts 16. Hamburg: L. Friederichsen.
sources.note: Duala-level (dual1243), not Oli-Bidiman. Vorwort p. V: words belonging to the neighbouring dialects 'Pongo, Mongo, Subu, Ewodi, Malimba u. a.' were excluded from the dictionary; Duala tones are set out (Hochton, Tiefton, Mittelton, plus Hochtief-, Tiefhoch-, Hochmittelton on one syllable). No mention of stress/Betonung/Akzent anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent), nothing on Ewodi/Oli or Bodiman phonology.

However, Oli-Bidiman is lexically (and otherwise) too distant from Duala to be intelligible (Carl Ebobissé 2014: 395, 409) to it, and thus merits an entry of its own.' Zero descriptive (grammar/phonology/sketch) references; the five refs are classification-only.

sources.note: Section II 'Les tons' (pp. 15-18) is placed before the phonemes because tone is 'une des caracteristiques essentielles du wori'. Wori is a tone language with two level tones (haut, bas); the tone-bearing segments are vowels and syllabic nasals; tones have demarcative and distinctive functions. HL and LH sequences on one syllable ('tons melodiques simples', analysed as two morae, no length contrast) are distinctive, giving four possibilities per syllable, but the author explicitly denies a 4-tone analysis.
